item.research_question: How does the indentation hardness of single-phase fcc FexNi1-x alloys vary with stoichiometry, and what microphysical mechanisms (specifically stacking fault energies and dislocation behavior) govern this variation?
item.material_system: Single-phase fcc FexNi1-x solid solutions (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) compared to elemental fcc-Fe and fcc-Ni
item.processing_route: Molecular dynamics simulation using the Bonny et al. potential; crystals created with random Fe/Ni placement on fcc lattice sites (66.4 nm lateral, 50.3 nm depth, ~20.8 million atoms); relaxed in NPT ensemble to ~1 mK; nanoindentation performed with a repulsive spherical indenter (R=10 nm, k=10 eV/Å3) moving at 20 m/s to a depth of 4 nm over 200 ps, held for 100 ps, then retracted at 20 m/s
item.test_conditions: Temperature: ~1 mK (to minimize thermal vibrations); Indenter velocity: 20 m/s; Final indentation depth: 4 nm; Time step: 1 fs; LAMMPS code with OVITO for analysis
key_findings: Indentation hardness is maximum for the equiatomic alloy (x=0.5), agreeing with experimental uniaxial strain results.
The unstable stacking fault energy (USFE) exhibits a maximum at intermediate stoichiometries (x=0.5), correlating directly with the hardness maximum.
Loop emission from the plastic zone becomes less pronounced with increasing Fe content; for pure fcc-Fe, only a single loop is ejected.
The total length of the dislocation network and the number of atoms in stacking faults within the plastic zone increase continuously with Fe content.
The volume of twinned regions is highest for elemental solids and decreases for the alloys due to inefficient concerted dislocation motion in concentrated compositions.
The fraction of screw dislocation segments in the plastic zone increases with Fe content, reaching high values in Fe-rich samples.
Surface imprints show increasing pile-up heights with increasing Fe content, with pure Fe exhibiting the highest hillocks.
The fraction of sessile dislocations (stair-rod, Hirth, Frank partials) reaches almost 20% for the equiatomic Fe50Ni50 alloy after tip retraction.
item.mechanism: The authors explain the hardness maximum at x=0.5 by the increase in unstable stacking fault energy (USFE), which quantifies the energy barrier for stacking fault creation and dislocation glide. The reduced loop emission and larger plastic zone in Fe-rich alloys are attributed to the difficulty of dislocation cross-slip required for loop formation. The suppression of twinning in alloys is explained by local compositional fluctuations reducing the probability of the concerted motion of dislocations on adjacent parallel lattice planes required for twin growth.
item.limitations: The authors note that small quantitative differences in indentation results are expected between the 1-mK simulation and room temperature experiments, though plasticity mechanisms remain unchanged. They also mention that previous studies using the Choi potential were not well-suited for this subsystem because it yielded negative SFE for pure Fe and monotonic USFE decrease.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the findings could be used for hardness engineering by creating gradient profiles in stoichiometry via ion implantation or plasma deposition to generate hardness profiles. They suggest experimental verification of the predicted extended dislocation semiloops and larger plastic zones in nano-pillars cut from single-phase FexNi1-x alloys or large single-crystalline grains.
quotes: The indentation hardness is maximum for the equiatomic alloy, x=0.5.
We explain this finding with the increase of the unstable stacking fault energy in the alloys towards x=0.5.
This concerted motion is less efficient in the alloys.
